Wendy Oxenhorn

Wendy Oxenhorn has contributed to jazz in America as an advocate, enthusiast, and a vital resource. In 2000 she became the Executive Director of the Jazz Foundation of America and she expanded their scope to musicians from 35 clients per year to 7,000 emergency assists per year. She has been honored numerous times, and received the 2016 NEA Lifetime Honors Jazz Masters Award.
Wendy was interviewed via Zoom on January 22, 2026 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

My name is Monk Rowe for the Fillius Jazz Archive and I’m very, very pleased to have Wendy Oxenhorn with me today. And you’ve presented a bit of a challenge as far as an introduction because you’ve done an awful lot in your life. So I came up – I don't know why I saw this but I’m going to call you the Red Cross for veteran jazz and blues musicians. How’s that?
And roots, and R&B, soul and rock & roll too.

Right. That is sort of one of my questions we’ll get to, but you were a co-founder and founding director of the Jazz Foundation. And I want to start right off with can you come up with a couple adjectives that describe that experience of, from the very get-go when you arrived at this foundation to where you are now. How would you describe the experience?
Oh, adjectives. Thrilling, challenging, exciting, creative.
You know I had written down a couple and you had two that I wrote down, because I was just trying to put myself in your position. Was there ever melancholy involved?

The melancholy came from two sources. One, how I even got the position and what I had been doing before that actually caused them to stand up and shake my hand at the job interview and say, “You’re it.” I had an interesting introduction to jazz. From the time I was a little kid I loved blues. I just loved blues and Billie Holiday, Frank Sinatra kind of jazz. And I used to listen with a transistor radio and swing on the swings and sing my heart out. You know. My biggest wish when I was like ten was to be a Raelette. You know ‘cause my parents used to love Ray Charles and listen and my mother one day like looked at me and she goes, “Wendy you can never be a Raelette.” I was like what? She goes, “You’re white.” And it was the first time in my life that I even realized that I wasn’t, you know, part of that club. And I remember, I remember being devastated you know. Because that’s really like that’s where I related. Those are the people I related to, that music was what I related to. I started out life as a ballerina. And you know when you dance, the only reason that you need to dance is because of music you know. I grew up, © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
even though I was a classical ballerina I grew up watching “Soul Train” on Saturdays trying to learn to dance like that you know. But anyway – it’s just –
May I ask, were there any black dancers in your ballet school and early career?

It’s a great question, there were only two. There were only two in the entire school and it was a very white business. And as a result you know it was something I never felt comfortable in that world. You know? But I loved to dance and ballet was what was open to me. That was the only thing that I was given at that time you know? And then I had a knee injury and I think it’s a well-known story that I was told I would never dance again, and that if I tried I’d be crippled by the time I was 30. So I ended up calling a suicide hotline and I started getting friendly with the counselor and I started asking how she was, and of course I ended up working there three days later. And by my having to save other people who were in depression, you know, it saved me, and that’s how I got my start in this world of doing good and helping those who suffer.

Before we leave that earlier in your life topic, can you describe the difference between, you know, swinging on a swing with a transistor radio and watching “Soul Train” and I would imagine you’re moving to it. How you move to that music seems to be fairly intrinsic and obvious. I mean there’s a groove there. So when you do ballet, the movement is not so obvious and it’s –
A very different groove.

It might come from a choreographer as well. The reason this popped into my head is for a short time we took our daughters to a dance instructor. And she would put on warm-up music and then have them do warm-up movements that had no relationship to the music. And so it used to irk me. Yet I realized I’m not schooled in that particular approach so, was ballet difficult for you in that the reaction to the music was not so obvious. I guess that was a long intro to a short question.

Well here’s the thing. The kind of music that you dance to in ballet can be gorgeous: Sibelius, and Mahler, and there are incredible – Erik Satie. You know there are incredible composers that can move you, and the kind of movement that you make, it’s going to be obviously far different. But there is a great beauty and a great expression in doing something slow and, you know bird-like. You know there’s beauty in the slowness and in, you know “The Swan.” Okay. But Saturday morning on “Soul Train,” like that was it. You know? That was like I wanted that. And I used to get in trouble in my ballet classes because you know I would try and do little things that just brought that into it you know. I would always get into trouble. But anyway, so when we talked about melancholy, so by the time I got to the Jazz Foundation job interview I had become a blues fan. I started playing blues in the train stations of New York City with an old man from Mississippi, and it was the greatest gift since my ballet. It was the first thing that I threw myself into. I © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

was mending my heart over a heartbreak and it was a musician who one of his instruments was the harmonica. So it was sitting on this table and one day we were listening to “Sugar Blue” and I picked it up and I started just – and he goes, you know, “Baby you got something.” And it was like I got bit by that. I would get on the trains, the express train from 96th Street to 14th Street – well my kids – I was a single parent – while my kids were in school. And I would play between the cars so I wouldn’t disturb anyone. I’d have Muddy Waters on, you know in my headphones, and I would just wail, like outside in the tunnel that connects the cars. So I’d be bouncing up and down holding on with one hand and just practicing my heart out. And then I met the old man, and that was it. I couldn’t have been happier and I started making enough money. I produced a little CD for us from our live recordings, and I started making enough money to support it. I was making like 800 a week off the books. Yes. You know, not too many little sidemen in New York can do that in the train station. Back in time for dinner. Didn’t even need a babysitter.
I’m going to pause for one second. Do you have a movable screen?
Oh, I do. Sorry. That’s my foot kicking the table?
No, no, no it’s not that. Can you bend it forward a little bit so that you’re higher in the picture?
Like that? Is that better?

That’s better, even a little more if you can. The reason for that is we do closed captions and – yeah, yeah. Okay. So I’ll just pick up from there. So did you have the little suitcase with all the different keys for the harmonica?

No, I could never afford all those harps. I could afford one, in the key that he was in, and there was only like one or two songs that I could do because of it. But really his purpose in inviting me to play with him – because at first I was just terrible – his purpose was to have a little blonde in a dress going to pass the tip bucket, and then when I became like an asset and I recorded us, and I was his CD partner and I was selling the CDs for 12 bucks apiece, we started rolling in the dough and that’s when, you know, my playing got much better. I would take this wailing solo. We would have like 50 people in the train station, this was just before 9/11 when people still gathered. And I would go sell the CDs while the song was still going on, I’d take my solo, and while we were in that moment I’d start selling the CDs and passing the tip bucket before the crowd dispersed. So I knew how to raise money, okay? That’s why the Jazz Foundation hired me.
I was going to say, did you put that on your resume? “Played blues in the subway.”

No, they knew my – that’s too funny – no I had a very successful – I had my 15 minutes of fame with another charity for the homeless selling the “Street News,” the newspapers that allowed the homeless to work and buy their own food, and that was successful and © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

they loved that. But when I told them, you know, I play blues in the train station with an old man from Mississippi. That was when the guy stood up and shook my hand and said, “You’re it.” But he forgot to tell me that I was the only person who showed up for the job interview.
Wow. In New York City. You were the only person, huh?

Yes. They advertised it in Psychology Today, which I don't know why, maybe it was all they could afford, but they offered me fifty big ones and I was very excited, I was a single parent. I had another part time job that I did besides the train station blues and when I left they called me back all week until the job at the Jazz Foundation said, “We want you back, we’ll start you at a hundred thousand.” And that was huge money back then. That was huge money to me you know, twenty years ago, whatever. And I could not even think about it. I was already bit by the mission of the foundation, the only thing was that when I started working at the foundation which I think you know, I found out there was only seven thousand dollars in the bank so there was no way they could pay me the fifty big ones. So I was really starting from scratch you know. The Foundation was founded by a few jazz enthusiasts including Billy Taylor and Herb Storfer, Bill Wurtzel and a few really – you know Sandy Jordan, which was Clifford Jordan’s wife, and I hope I’m not leaving out too many people but Jimmy Owens and the only issue was that they were just people that were well intended but they didn’t really – they had never run an organization before and they turned it halfway through it was just going to be an archival organization, sort of like what you do. And they turned it into an emergency fund because Vishnu Wood and Jamil Nasser, and Jimmy Owens came to them and said, “There’s all these musicians having terrible issues. We need to do something.” And that’s how it turned into it. But I think in four years they’d only helped 35 musicians. And they were going under because Herb Storfer was 80 now and he could no longer do this. So they put an ad in the paper and, you know in the magazine, and there you go.

Was there a sort of, I’m going to use the word “triage” when a person was presented or came to you or was brought to the organization, was there an assessment like what do we need immediately and what could be the long-term plan for this person.

Honestly they just said, “Here are the keys to the office, you’re going to have to be a one- man band because we don’t have money to hire anyone else. And I looked through, there were tons of boxes and I looked through just to see – there wasn’t even a procedure on how to help. There wasn’t even a questionnaire. So it really was fabulous because you know what I neglected to tell you was that the old man in the train station that I played with got himself a girlfriend 15 years younger than him. It was his first woman in a long time. And she wanted to sing with the band. She fired me. So I was without my job, like I was without my blues. That was how I was feeding my children. And the blues was like © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

the love of my life. You know? So you have to understand the sequence. So here I was without the blues and then look what happened because of that experience, because of taking care of the old man, building a business, getting him to be financially independent from the blues. I was able to have what I needed to relate, and also having been a musician for the year. You know I worked in the train stations where when it was sweltering, you know, the old man used to keep a bag of ice under his little bowler hat. You know I mean in the winter we would get frostbite, you know I couldn’t even hold the harmonica many times when it was cold in the train station. And we had the experience of incredible racism. When we were asked to do the street festivals they’d hire a better known band, and we’re not even talking a famous band but they’d have an all-white band and they’d have a stage for them and they’d make the blues band, you know me, the old man or a Japanese guitarist and this great drummer used to play for Jimi Hendrix at Small’s Paradise. They would make us play on the pavement in the street without shade over our head for three hours for a hundred bucks for the whole band. You know? When it would rain we couldn’t go under the protection of the stage. So there were a lot of things I gleaned from that experience. And I also knew what it was like to have part times getting by and being very proud and never asking for help because as a single parent in New York City forget it. You know you become very resourceful. So it really gave me I think more than an MBA, it gave me a lot of experience and knowledge that I never could have gotten another way – to help people who were in the same situation.

It makes me think of John Levy, who managed Joe Williams and Nancy Wilson and Cannonball Adderley. And he had been a musician, he had been a bassist with a number of people and I know Joe used to say, “Well that made him a good manager for me because he knew the routine. He knew the challenges and how to deal with musicians, etcetera.”
Yeah.
So when you decided seven thousand dollars isn’t going to go too far.
Yeah I had to start working for free before I could help anyone.
Did it occur to you that maybe the best way to support these veteran musicians who had some troubles was to reach out to the musicians who were doing fairly well and could help out?
Wait, say that again?
Well I’m wondering, if you had came up with the Great Night in Harlem and how did that idea come to you?

Oh well you know I knew we needed a lot of money. I started seeing that the musicians were really in a bad way and because they were so proud, no one would ever come and ask for help. You had to hear someone was having a hard time through someone else. So © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

I was – you know I knew nothing really about jazz. And I didn’t have, I mean I left school for the ballet, I left school after ninth grade. That was the highest education I had. So I, you know there weren’t like research studies I did on helping people, I had not become a licensed social worker, but my time at the hotline, the suicide hotline, I had been counseling for years and I had a few other organizations not just helping the homeless but kids and people in rough situations. So I had a lot of counseling experience. And I was very intuitive. So it was easy to know how to help the musicians because they thought like me. You know? They were all living on the fringe for years, they were very resourceful, they were creative, and they always thought outside the box. So finding ways to help them was so easy for both of us. Because they knew, you know I was very clear in the fact that I had been at one point living on eight dollars a day with two kids. You know? When I was starting my charities in the past I didn’t have family money to back it up, I was just going raw, just like they do for the love of what they do so they could see that I really, genuinely had been in their position and I really understood. So I was able to say to them, “I’m buying you groceries today and you’re going to accept it, because, you know, and then we would laugh later that night when I’d call them and they’d be eating, you know, tuna fish sandwiches when they had just had a jar of pickles in the fridge and a bunch of ketchup packets. You know and the only reason I knew was ‘cause I would go to their homes. You know they never tell you anything like really, so the only way to really discover how someone’s doing would be to go visit them. And you’d have a great excuse, “I was in the ‘hood taking care of someone else” which was good. That meant that I’m not there just for them so they don’t feel like they’re a charitable case you know. I was there and we had such a great talk on the phone I just wanted to come by and say hello and I remembered you said sardines you loved so I brought some. You know? And the door opened and we would talk for an hour, and then I would just happen to get myself something from the fridge, and say, “Oh I’m just going to grab something” you know some water or ice cubes or whatever. And then I’d get to see what was in it. And then I’d get to really go shopping and we’d get to make a list of what they wanted and I would tell them I went through the same thing and someone did this for me so I’m just passing it on and I’m going to do it for you. You know and it was just – there was a soul connection that was truly magical and beautiful. And what was so ironic was a lot of these people were the people that my love affair that he used to take me to hear, these were his idols. So I learned about some of them before, even though I knew nothing about jazz I learned by going. You know? And hearing. Being taken to hear somebody. And then the most circular amazing experiences with me ending up getting to save the very person that we had gone to hear, who my soulmate had loved and was in awe of, and me this little single parent with two kids end up being able to have the honor and © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

privilege of makes me tearful, you know, to think about who these people were. These were the pioneers of the music. These were the original freedom fighters. These were the people who found a way out of the racism because in Europe these people, in America you know you’re talking about the amount of racism we had while they were in the height of their careers, and in Europe they were kings and queens. These were brilliant people who recreated an entire and reinvented an existence for them where they got to be acknowledged for who they truly are and the beauty they contributed to this world you know. I’m sorry, go ahead.

Did you ever get involved in trying to recover, and this is a legal avenue sort of, trying to recover owed payments or royalties for things that they had written that they had been cheated out of? Was that part of what you ended up doing?

It’s funny you should put it that way but there was really not much recourse. There were contracts they signed with labels, record companies, for their own publishing that they could never get. I remember a musician telling me a very famous label, when he said that he wanted his own publishing the executive said to him, “No,” – and I’m not going to use the N word – but he said, “No N is going to ever have his own publishing while I’m alive.” You know? This is how it was when you recorded with someone like Frank Sinatra, you know, the horn section. You got three hundred dollars for the gig, for the recording, and then there were no royalties on the vinyl that was sold. There was nothing else. So you got to pay your rent once. And then CDs were invented, there was nothing in contracts, CDs weren’t invented yet. There was nothing to cover people. It would have been wonderful if there was a class action suit that could do something like that but I don’t think there was anyone interested and if they were I do know there were record labels would often try to buy out attorneys, just like in divorces you hear of this. You know? The rich husband goes to the lawyer the wife is using and does something to make it a conflict of interest for him to be able to represent her. You know I think there had to be payoffs, things like that. I’m not going to assume but you know it wasn’t done, so what I would tell the musicians when they had a hard time accepting help from the Jazz Foundation was think of this as all the money that you never got that you should have when you were cheated by clubs that didn’t pay properly or promoters that took advantage of you when you were on the road, all the hotels that should have been covered for you while you were touring, the food that should have been covered for you, you know and you come back almost breaking even from a European tour. That they were able to absolutely assimilate and say okay, that I can do.

I used to be quite naïve about my musical heroes and jazz musicians in general thinking that because I saw their names on LPs and in concerts for a long time I assumed that they © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
sort of “had it made.” Like all they had to do was play jazz gigs and they made a lot of money. And one time I had interviewed Gene Bertoncini, and he happened to mention –
Oh, my boyfriend – I love him. I think he’s almost a hundred and still playing.
The next day he was playing a wedding. And I said, “You’re playing a wedding?” Like I mean I know this stuff because I’m a musician too.
[Inaudible] record albums.
Yeah, right. And Milt Hinton and these fellas who played on these rock & roll records and all that, the story is completely fascinating to me.

It’s beyond. And we know all the earlier racism, everyone knows the clubs, the labels, the record companies, we know so many things that went down back then. There was one story that really stands out in my early moments, and I’ll segue into the Great Night in Harlem and answer your question, but there was a legend who – I think it was Ron Carter who came to me and said, “I ran into someone at the airport and he didn’t have a seeing eye cane but he was blind as a bat, he really couldn’t see where he was going.” And this was like a serious legend who had recorded with everyone. He said, “I asked him where he was coming back from and he had been in Greece for one night for five hundred dollars.” And Ron Carter took him in his car and drove him two hours back to his home in Jersey or Pennsylvania. And he said, “You’ve got to get in touch with this guy, he needs us.” So I called him and we started speaking and he said – “I don’t need any help, lady.” You know. So we got to the subject of how is he eating, how is he shopping. He can’t drive. So he lived a block away from a 7-Eleven and he was drinking those cans of Ensure and M&Ms, eating M&Ms. So I found out he’d been doing that for over a year. So I suggested, because we didn’t have a lot of money then but I suggested Meals on Wheels. And he was like, “I don’t need any kind of help, lady” and he hung up on me. And I was like oh man. So I called him back the next day and I said, “Listen,” I said, I worried about you all night. I didn’t sleep you know. I said, “We got tight on the phone, we were telling, we were comparing stories.” I was telling of some of the old man train station blues stories and we were laughing. And I said, “I’m going to be worrying about you now.” And I was talking into his machine. He didn’t pick up. And then all of a sudden the receiver picks up, he goes, “Wendy, I don’t want you to worry about me.” I said, “Well then I’m going to ask you one favor in our relationship would you promise me, would you try, just once would you try, this places delivers good meals like twice a day, lunch and dinner. Just try it once. Okay? Just so that I’ll sleep.” You know. So he agreed. He called up later the next day after they made their first visit. And he was just like over the moon. He said it had been so long since I had like real food. And he was just like so full of energy and happiness, and he loved the woman who delivered it. She sat and talked with him. He had no company. You know? And after that like his energy was © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

coming back and I introduced him, I asked him to do a gig with this young musician and they got tight. And before we knew it young musicians were asking him to sit in at clubs. So he would guest star. So he was making money. They were getting paid more because they had the famous name and they were becoming like family. So this became a little thing that started happening with some of the elders. So many beautiful things. So okay, Great Night in Harlem. I really didn’t know anything about jazz. In fact I could tell you that up until a couple of years ago I mean it’s so embarrassing, but I thought, I’m not even going to say it, but there was a great legend who was a piano player, I mean he was a saxophonist, and I thought he was a piano player. Okay? I thought he played piano, okay? So just there you go. So I wanted to learn about jazz and I watched the Jean Bach documentary, “A Great Day in Harlem.” So I figured I’ll learn about everyone. And I thought to myself wouldn’t it be incredible to get all the living legends together and do a great night in Harlem. And do it in Harlem. So I thought of the Apollo Theater. But it was like fifteen thousand dollars at the time to rent it, and no one had done jazz or blues there in like I think it was 30 or 50 years. So I went back to my board and I told them this great idea and they said, “Wendy, first of all we’re not concert producers. You’re not a concert producer. We can’t do this. Plus we don’t have fifteen thousand dollars.” So I said, “Okay, listen, why don’t we look into getting someone who maybe could do that, who knows how to do that.” So we interviewed one person and she wanted a hundred thousand dollars to do it. So we were like okay let’s do this the Wendy way, okay, like the single parent Wendy way. So I said, “Do we know anyone with money? And Herb Storfer, the original founder who I love, he was the 80-year-old who could no longer help the musicians. He would, by the way, pull money out of his pocket. If someone had a heart attack they’d come to his apartment. That’s how the Jazz Foundation used to run. And he would give them five hundred for their rent. The guy was a saint. And so they said, he said, “I know one rich person” and he said, “my neighbor.” And he loves the little events we have in my apartment.” I said, “Okay, good, what is he?” He goes, “I think he’s a merchant banker.” So I got in touch with the guy the next day. We went to lunch. And I told him what was happening, I told him where we were, the kind of need these great musicians – turned out that he was learning blues guitar on his own, he loved the music, he loved the whole idea, and he goes, “I’ll give the 15 thousand dollars for the rent of the Apollo.” I was like woo-hoo. So we were on our way. Now there was no way I could do this alone, so I think I went to George Wein’s Festival Productions and asked, because George Wein had known of what we were doing. He never thought the idea would go well because he said it’s going to be a bottomless pit. These guys can’t – their medical costs alone would be – nobody would have enough money for that. When I told him what we were doing, what was happening, the musicians that were getting helped, he © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

was like this is incredible. “I’m going to give you my top producer.” And he gave us Rick White which was amazing, and Dan Melnick. And then some of the guys on our board, Bob Cranshaw and Jimmy Owens, they started reaching out to musicians. At the time I asked if anyone knew anyone famous. Someone had the number for Bill Cosby’s agent, so I left word. I remember a week later I get a call and I hear this guy with this voice that sounds familiar go, “Wendy?” I was like, “Yes.” He goes, “This is Cos.” Okay. This is before anyone knew what he was up to in his spare time. But to us in that time he was a big star yet, the Cosby show, that was like an A list name that was like Whoopi Goldberg to us, you know. So we got Cos, he said he’d do it and it just started snowballing. And we had only nine weeks to put it together. I told the board I have to hire someone because I cannot continue to do this alone. I was doing the emergencies, I was doing the bookkeeping, which I was terrible. I was raising the money, I was starting to recruit a board, I was doing the events, I was doing the marketing. It was insane. So they told me we could get an intern. So I contacted a friend of mine and he was teaching African studies in – oh I forgot the university, Adam Gusso, but he was an amazing guy. He also played harmonica with an all-blues band. And he sent one of his students who turned out to be the most brilliant young woman. She looked like she could be a little church girl from Atlanta. And it turned out she ended up leaving us to become an attorney. She got a full ride to Northeastern. She was just incredible. Lauren Roberts. And the two of us in nine weeks put this together. And 13 days before our first Great Night in Harlem we had – oh I think it was over a hundred of the living legends at the time coming together. Freddie Hubbard, I mean everyone. And 9/11 happened 13 days before. So we thought okay no one’s going to show. The house was packed. We had a four hour concert and we raised $350,000.
That’s amazing.
So we were in business.
Who was in charge of assembling the combos, the combinations of people?

I think that was Rick White from Festival Productions and Dan Melnick. Yeah. Rick White was amazing. I think he’s teaching at Columbia. But yeah, it was just – and honestly you know how things like that happen. It was – it just happened. You know? And you get all those people coming together, the reunion that was happening backstage. And I remember I got this photographer, John Abbott, and I still have yet to ask him for a copy or I lost it over the years, but I asked him to do a photo of a Great Night in Harlem that night. And he got on the ledge of the first balcony and he took, there must have been a hundred of the greats. Everybody came on stage. And I didn’t go for the photo because I didn’t think I had earned that right. You know? © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
I sort of know what you mean. I’ve been in company with some of these people like Milt Hinton and there’s something about their glow, they’re like magnets.
They’re incredible.
People want to stand next to them because they make you feel better.

Well it’s their vibration that they –the frequency that they vibrate from. You know? They said, I can’t remember if it was Leonard Cohen or Bob Dylan said that the music is up there and we just bring it down. You know? Musicians bring it down. And I do believe that with all my heart. You know? They are healers. You know? The musicians are the healers of the world and I can’t imagine getting through life, and I always used to say that to our audience, you know they were there when you fell in love and they were there when you got divorced. The music is what got us through life. So it ended up becoming a very beautiful – it wasn’t a job, it was a way of life. It was like a sacred task to usher and transition these people at a time in life at an age where they had been forgotten, the phone didn’t ring, they couldn’t do three hour, three sets anymore. There was incapacitation. No one had money or insurance for doctors you know. Once you’re of Medicare age, you know, it’s generally too late. You can have advanced stages of cancer. Don’t forget there was smoking for years in the clubs. You know all sorts of things that affected their health you know. Sorry, that’s another creditor.
Do you consider yourself an optimist?
Oh yes.
I thought you’d say oh yes. This is a little off topic, but does your optimism include the wider view of our country at the moment?

Woo. Bigger question. Let’s put it this way. I believe that there are consequences for all actions and this country was founded on not just racism but murder, but stolen lives.
